transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick intros?
[00:08] Jasmine (Aurora): Hi, Jasmine here, head of MLOps at Aurora, Tom and Priya on from infra and security.
[00:15] Alex: Awesome. Priya Shah from Redwood SE will lead the technical pieces. Priya, take it away.
[00:23] Priya (Redwood SE): Thanks. So agenda: artifact delivery, GPU driver licensing for air-gapped installs, runtime performance around KV cache & batching, quantization tradeoffs, and integration with KMS/VPC. We'll pause for Qs.
[00:38] Tom (Aurora Infra): Our constraints: strict air-gap, no outbound internet from the inference cluster, and compliance requires that only signed artifacts are installed. We also have mixed GPUs — A100s and some older A40s.
[00:52] Priya: Great, that matches common setups. For artifact delivery we usually provide two paths: signed tarball + checksums you fetch via secure courier, or a physical USB/SSD image delivered with an HSM-signed manifest. Both include the runtime, model weights, and driver installers where licensing allows.
[01:10] Priya: Note — GPU driver licensing can be tricky. Some vendors require online activation or vendor-specific offline license tokens. In our experience, NVIDIA driver packages can be delivered offline but enterprise licensed driver features (like MIG or specific support bundles) sometimes need a license file. We work with partner processes to get vendor-signed license files that you can install locally.
[01:30] Priya: For customers that cannot accept vendor-supplied binaries, we can also provide a validated build recipe and checksums for you to build in your secure CI, then send us the attestation. That's heavier but possible.
[01:40] Jasmine: When you say "provide driver installers where licensing allows" — can you clarify what Redwood takes responsibility for vs what we must procure?
[01:48] Alex: Generally, Redwood provisions the runtime and the inference engine, and we can include vendor drivers only if we have a redistribution agreement. If not, we hand you the exact package names and checksums and the steps to obtain the vendor license yourself. We'll be explicit in the delivery options.
[02:05] Tom: Our procurement won't allow us to accept drivers copied from third-party sources; we need vendor-signed drivers.
[02:12] Priya: Understood. We'll add both flows in the artifact delivery doc; option A: Redwood provides vendor-licensed driver bundle (if agreement in place), option B: customer obtains from vendor and we provide install automation and checksums.
[02:26] Evan (Data Scientist): On the runtime performance side, curious about KV cache behavior across long-running chat sessions and batch size tradeoffs — our models have 2k-4k context and lots of short sessions.
[02:36] Priya: Good question. Our runtime uses a continuous KV cache for active sessions; for short sessions the overhead of cache lookups is very small. For long contexts we shard KV cache across GPU memory and use eviction policies to prioritize recent tokens. The key is batching policy: if you set a tight latency SLO we'll keep batch windows small; for throughput runs we can increase batching to amortize kernel launch costs.
[03:05] Jasmine: Any numbers you can share — like RPS or median token latency differences when enabling aggressive batching?
[03:12] Priya: Ballpark: on A100s with 8k context and quantized 4-bit weights, single-request latency for a 50-token completion is ~70-110ms median without batching; enabling batching (batch=8) can increase median to ~120-180ms but throughput improves 6-8x. These are workload-dependent. We'll provide bench numbers for your prompts.
[03:34] Tom: How does quantization affect output quality? Our clinical team cares about hallucination risks.
[03:40] Priya: We recommend a two-path approach: performance-critical endpoints can use 4-bit quantization with regular quality checks, and a small percentage of requests can use fp16 or fp32 to validate quality. Redwood Optimize suggests per-route quantization profiles. For many open models, 4-bit post-training quantization with activation clipping has minimal impact on rouge/accuracy for classification-ish tasks, but you should run your task-specific evals.
[04:05] Priya: Also note quantization reduces memory footprint, which can let you run larger context or more concurrent streams on the same GPU.
[04:12] Jasmine: Interesting. For our use, accuracy is paramount — we'll want to keep a small canary of fp16.
[04:18] Alex: Totally reasonable. We can configure route-level overrides so 95% uses quantized and 5% goes to higher-precision.
[04:26] Tom: Back to drivers — offline licensing: how do you handle driver updates and security patches if the cluster is air-gapped?
[04:33] Priya: We recommend a quarterly maintenance cadence. We provide a patch manifest and signed packages; customers apply patches in their staging air-gapped environment, run smoke tests, then promote to prod. For critical CVEs we can accelerate and coordinate an emergency release and a courier delivery. We also provide a checklist for vendor-specific mitigations.
[04:51] Priya: On the install side we ship an installer image that contains: runtime binaries, model shard loader, recommended driver versions, and a manifest with sha256 sums. Installation is executed via our offline installer CLI which validates the manifests and rejects mismatches.
[05:05] Priya: Important caveat — certain GPU features (e.g., MIG multi-instance or proprietary telemetry) depend on vendor driver versions. We'll document the supported driver versions and the tradeoffs.
[05:16] Priya: Now on networking and KMS: for air-gapped KMS, we support bring-your-own HSM or KMS inside the VPC. Keys are used to unlock the model weights at boot; the decryption step happens locally and we avoid key egress. We support policy-based key rotation and audit logging.
[05:33] Priya: If you require HSM-backed signing of artifacts, we can sign manifests on our side and provide the public verification key. If you require local signing only, we support an attestable build flow.
[05:45] Priya: Any questions on KMS?
[05:49] Priya Nair (Security): Does Redwood's audit log capture token-level usage if everything is private? We need to provide access logs for compliance.
[05:56] Miguel (CSM): Yes — the private deployment includes local telemetry and an audit log collector. Logs are stored locally or forwarded to your SIEM; we can also ship a read-only export. We never egress usage data unless explicitly configured.
[06:10] Jasmine: For the bench test, what do you need from us?
[06:14] Priya: Ideally list of target nodes, OS images, GPU firmware versions, and a short corpus of representative prompts. We'll run both single-request latency tests and heavy throughput workloads with varying batch sizes and quantization settings.
[06:27] Evan: We'll include clinical QA prompts plus a set of short chat interactions — about 5k tokens total.
[06:32] Priya: Perfect. We'll also instrument KV cache hit/miss rates and memory pressure so you can see how eviction behaves.
[06:40] Tom: What about fallback policies? If a driver mismatch causes a node to fail, can Redwood route to hosted or dedicated while we remediate?
[06:48] Alex: Yes — Redwood has smart routing and fallback policies. For enterprise customers we typically enable a fallback to a staged model variant on a different capacity tier. For air-gapped customers that cannot call out, we recommend a standby cluster or a canary lanes approach; we can help design failover patterns.
[07:04] Jasmine: Any examples of issues during on-prem installs?
[07:07] Priya: Common ones: mismatched CUDA/cuDNN versions, driver feature toggles, or incorrect manifest checksums. We mitigate these with pre-check scripts and a dry-run installer that validates the environment before installing.
[07:20] Priya: We'll include a preflight checklist to verify kernel modules, secure boot settings, and required kernel flags.
[07:27] Tom: About secure delivery — can we require courier with tamper-evident packaging and chain-of-custody forms?
[07:33] Alex: Absolutely; we can add chain-of-custody and options for notarized delivery. We worked with customers using the same process for regulated workloads.
[07:41] Jasmine: On licensing costs, are there extra fees for Redwood to redistribute vendor drivers?
[07:46] Alex: Redistribution agreements vary. If we need to obtain redistribution rights from the GPU vendor, that cost is typically passed through or included as an add-on line item in the enterprise purchase order. We'll be transparent in the quote.
[07:58] Priya: For the runtime itself we support multiple quantization backends; if you prefer a specific quantization scheme (e.g., GPTQ vs AWQ) we can run A/Bs during the bench. Each has different perf/quality tradeoffs.
[08:12] Evan: Good to know. Also can we get token-level cost estimates for different batch sizes?
[08:18] Alex: We'll provide a cost model based on throughput and GPU utilization from the bench results. Redwood Console also surfaces per-token cost and latency breakdown in private deployments.
[08:29] Priya: Next, quick demo of our offline installer UX (brief): the CLI computes checksums, validates signatures against a provided public key, and runs a dry-run. During install it records a signed installation attestation you can keep for audits.
[08:46] Priya: (demo commentary) if checksum fails the installer aborts and writes a diagnostic bundle.
[08:52] Tom: Good — can we plug that diagnostic bundle into our internal ticketing?
[08:56] Miguel: Yes, the diagnostic bundle is a tar.gz with logs and a small JSON summary; we can adapt formatting for your ticket ingestor.
[09:05] Jasmine: OK, let's recap and confirm next steps.
[09:09] Alex: Recap: Redwood to share offline artifact options and signed manifest, SE to run bench plan once Aurora provides nodes & prompts, CSM to share SOC2 & install playbook, customer provides procurement constraints and GPU images.
[09:22] Jasmine: Sounds good. Any blockers?
[09:25] Tom: We need to confirm vendor driver procurement timeline; procurement may take 2-3 weeks.
[09:31] Alex: Noted. We'll schedule the bench for the week of 2026-04-06 to allow procurement.
[09:37] Priya: I'll follow up with a bench checklist and a small set of sample scripts.
[09:42] Jasmine: Thanks, everyone.
[09:44] Alex: Thanks — we'll send the docs and proposed bench times.
[09:48] (call ends)
